topic: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: The mole
subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement about one mole of a substance is correct?
items.correct: It contains 6.02 × 10²³ of whichever entity is specified.
items.misconception: It has a mass of 12 g, whichever substance it may be.
items.why: In everyday English 'amount' means 'how much', usually judged by weighing, and the mole was defined for many years through 12 g of carbon-12, so '12 g' is remembered as what a mole is. Confusion of amount of substance with mass is widely reported in research on teaching the mole. Keep the three quantities apart: amount n in mol (a count), mass m in g, and molar mass M in g mol⁻¹ that links them, n = m/M. A number with the unit mol cannot be put where a mass in g is needed, or read as g, without multiplying by M.
items.specStatementText: The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly the number of elementary entities given by the Avogadro constant.
items.random_wrong: It contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms, whatever the substance.

items.q: How many atoms are there in 0.500 mol of water, H₂O? (N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
items.why:
First examples use elements or ask for molecules, so N = n × N_A is learned as 'the number of particles' without asking which particle. The loose word 'particles' in many textbooks hides the difference. Identify the entity whose amount n refers to (usually the formula unit), and the entity the question asks for. Number of atoms = n(formula units) × atoms per formula unit × N_A; the same applies to ions and electrons.

Working: N(molecules) = n × N_A = 0.500 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 3.01 × 10²³. Each H₂O molecule contains 2 H + 1 O = 3 atoms, so N(atoms) = 3 × 3.01 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²³.
items.specStatementText: The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly the number of elementary entities given by the Avogadro constant.
items.working: N(molecules) = n × N_A = 0.500 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 3.01 × 10²³. Each H₂O molecule contains 2 H + 1 O = 3 atoms, so N(atoms) = 3 × 3.01 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²³.

items.q: How many electrons are there in 0.200 mol of ammonia, NH₃? (N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; atomic numbers: H 1, N 7)
items.why:
Lewis formulas and dot-and-cross diagrams draw only the outer electrons, so students take them as showing all the electrons present. The number of electrons in a neutral molecule is the sum of the atomic numbers of its atoms. Lewis formulas omit inner electrons because they take no part in bonding, not because they are absent.

Working: Electrons per NH₃ molecule = Z(N) + 3 × Z(H) = 7 + 3 = 10. N(electrons) = 0.200 mol × 10 × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.204 × 10²⁴ ≈ 1.20 × 10²⁴.
items.specStatementText: The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly the number of elementary entities given by the Avogadro constant.
items.working: Electrons per NH₃ molecule = Z(N) + 3 × Z(H) = 7 + 3 = 10. N(electrons) = 0.200 mol × 10 × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.204 × 10²⁴ ≈ 1.20 × 10²⁴.

items.q: A student writes: 'M_r of carbon dioxide, CO₂ = 44.01 g mol⁻¹'. Which comment on this statement is correct?
items.correct: The unit is wrong: M_r is a ratio of masses, with no unit.
items.misconception: It is correct: M_r and molar mass are one and the same quantity.
items.why: The two share the same number, and the terms are used interchangeably in many sources and in everyday talk in laboratories, so the unit of one is transferred to the other. Use M_r (no unit) when comparing masses of particles and M (g mol⁻¹) in n = m/M. Writing the unit is a quick check of which quantity is meant.
items.specStatementText: Masses of atoms are compared on a scale relative to ¹²C and are expressed as relative atomic mass A_r and relative formula mass M_r.
items.random_wrong: The unit is wrong: M_r is the mass of one molecule in grams.

items.q: The mass of one molecule of compound Z is 3.666 times the mass of one atom of carbon-12. What is the relative molecular mass, M_r, of Z?
items.why:
The word 'relative' suggests a straight comparison with the reference atom, and the factor of one twelfth in the definition is easily lost. On the A_r scale, carbon-12 is 12, not 1. Compare the particle with one twelfth of a ¹²C atom, or multiply its ratio to a whole ¹²C atom by 12.

Working: On the relative mass scale one ¹²C atom = 12 exactly. M_r(Z) = (mass of Z molecule ÷ mass of ¹²C atom) × 12 = 3.666 × 12 = 43.992 ≈ 43.99.
items.specStatementText: Masses of atoms are compared on a scale relative to ¹²C and are expressed as relative atomic mass A_r and relative formula mass M_r.
items.working: On the relative mass scale one ¹²C atom = 12 exactly. M_r(Z) = (mass of Z molecule ÷ mass of ¹²C atom) × 12 = 3.666 × 12 = 43.992 ≈ 43.99.

items.q: How many ions are there in 5.55 g of calcium chloride, CaCl₂? (N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; A_r: Cl 35.45, Ca 40.08)
items.why:
Cl₂ is met first as the formula of chlorine gas, and ionic formulae are read as though they were molecular; research on ionic bonding reports that many students picture ionic compounds as built from molecules. In an ionic formula each subscript counts separate ions. Work out the ions from their charges: Ca²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ ions for neutrality, so 1 mol of CaCl₂ contains 3 mol of ions.

Working: M(CaCl₂) = 40.08 + 2(35.45) = 110.98 g mol⁻¹. n = m/M = 5.55 g ÷ 110.98 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0500 mol. Ions per formula unit = 1 Ca²⁺ + 2 Cl⁻ = 3. N(ions) = 0.0500 × 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²².
items.specStatementText: Molar mass M has the units g mol⁻¹.

items.q: The relative molecular mass of methane, CH₄, is 16.05. Which statement about the molar mass, M, of methane is correct?
items.correct: It is 16.05 g mol⁻¹; 1 mol of CH₄ molecules has mass 16.05 g.
items.misconception: It is 16.05 g; one molecule of CH₄ has a mass of 16.05 g.
items.why: Relative masses are first met on the periodic table as 'the mass of an atom', and grams enter later through molar mass; students merge the two and lose the factor of N_A between one particle and one mole. A single particle has a mass of the order of 10⁻²³ g. Grams go with a mole of particles: M in g mol⁻¹. The relative mass M_r has no unit at all.
items.specStatementText: Molar mass M has the units g mol⁻¹.
items.random_wrong: It is 16.05, with no unit, as molar mass is the same as M_r.

items.q: An oxide of iron contains 69.94% iron and 30.06% oxygen by mass. Which ratio of iron atoms to oxygen atoms gives its empirical formula? (A_r: O 16.00, Fe 55.85)
items.why:
Students are told that experimental ratios come out 'close to' whole numbers and should be rounded, and they apply this to values such as 1.50 that are far from a whole number. Round only values that are very close to a whole number (such as 2.98 to 3). A value near .5, .33, .67 or .25 means every value must be multiplied by 2, 3 or 4.

Working: n(Fe) = 69.94 ÷ 55.85 = 1.252 mol; n(O) = 30.06 ÷ 16.00 = 1.879 mol (per 100 g). Divide by the smaller: Fe 1.00, O 1.879 ÷ 1.252 = 1.50. Multiply by 2: Fe : O = 2 : 3, so the empirical formula is Fe₂O₃.
items.specStatementText: The empirical formula of a compound gives the simplest ratio of atoms of each element present in that compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element present in a molecule.
items.working: n(Fe) = 69.94 ÷ 55.85 = 1.252 mol; n(O) = 30.06 ÷ 16.00 = 1.879 mol (per 100 g). Divide by the smaller: Fe 1.00, O 1.879 ÷ 1.252 = 1.50. Multiply by 2: Fe : O = 2 : 3, so the empirical formula is Fe₂O₃.

items.q: What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄? (A_r: H 1.01, N 14.01, O 16.00, S 32.07)
items.why:
Inside a formula a subscript applies only to the symbol just before it, and students extend that rule to a number after a bracket. Expand the bracket before counting: (NH₄)₂SO₄ = N₂H₈SO₄. Brackets group atoms that the multiplier applies to as a unit, such as a polyatomic ion or an empirical formula unit.

Working: M_r((NH₄)₂SO₄) = 2 × (14.01 + 4 × 1.01) + 32.07 + 4 × 16.00 = 36.10 + 32.07 + 64.00 = 132.17. Mass of N per formula unit = 2 × 14.01 = 28.02. % N = 28.02 ÷ 132.17 × 100 = 21.20%.
items.specStatementText: The empirical formula of a compound gives the simplest ratio of atoms of each element present in that compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element present in a molecule.

items.q: The empirical formula of ethanoic acid is CH₂O. What does this empirical formula tell you about ethanoic acid?
items.correct: Its atoms of C, H and O are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1.
items.misconception: Each of its molecules has one C atom, two H atoms and one O atom.
items.why: Many compounds met early (H₂O, CO₂, NH₃, CH₄) have identical empirical and molecular formulae, so students do not see why a separate molar mass step is needed. Composition data fix only the ratio of atoms, C : H = 2 : 3, which is the same for C₄H₆, C₈H₁₂ and C₁₂H₁₈. The molar mass selects one of them: x = M ÷ empirical formula mass.
items.specStatementText: The empirical formula of a compound gives the simplest ratio of atoms of each element present in that compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element present in a molecule.
items.random_wrong: The masses of its C, H and O are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1.

items.q: A hydrocarbon contains 88.80% carbon and 11.20% hydrogen by mass. Its molar mass is 54.10 g mol⁻¹. What is its molecular formula? (A_r: H 1.01, C 12.01)
items.correct: C₄H₆
items.misconception: C₂H₃
items.why:
Many compounds met early (H₂O, CO₂, NH₃, CH₄) have identical empirical and molecular formulae, so students do not see why a separate molar mass step is needed. Composition data fix only the ratio of atoms, C : H = 2 : 3, which is the same for C₄H₆, C₈H₁₂ and C₁₂H₁₈. The molar mass selects one of them: x = M ÷ empirical formula mass.

Working: Per 100 g: n(C) = 88.80 ÷ 12.01 = 7.394 mol; n(H) = 11.20 ÷ 1.01 = 11.09 mol. Ratio H : C = 11.09 ÷ 7.394 = 1.50, so C : H = 1 : 1.50 = 2 : 3 and the empirical formula is C₂H₃. Empirical formula mass = 2(12.01) + 3(1.01) = 27.05. x = 54.10 ÷ 27.05 = 2.00. Molecular formula = (C₂H₃)₂ = C₄H₆.
items.specStatementText: The empirical formula of a compound gives the simplest ratio of atoms of each element present in that compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element present in a molecule.
items.working: Per 100 g: n(C) = 88.80 ÷ 12.01 = 7.394 mol; n(H) = 11.20 ÷ 1.01 = 11.09 mol. Ratio H : C = 11.09 ÷ 7.394 = 1.50, so C : H = 1 : 1.50 = 2 : 3 and the empirical formula is C₂H₃. Empirical formula mass = 2(12.01) + 3(1.01) = 27.05. x = 54.10 ÷ 27.05 = 2.00. Molecular formula = (C₂H₃)₂ = C₄H₆.

items.q: What amount of sodium hydroxide is present in 25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) in which [NaOH] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³?
items.why:
The conversion factor for length is applied to volume without cubing it, a unit error widely reported in science and mathematics education. Cube the length factor for a volume: (10 cm)³ = 1000 cm³. A 1 dm³ bottle holds 1000 cm³ (1 litre).

Working: V = 25.0 cm³ ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³. n = CV = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.0250 dm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol = 0.00250 mol.
items.specStatementText: The molar concentration is determined by the amount of solute and the volume of solution.

items.q: Which procedure produces a solution in which [NaCl] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³? (M(NaCl) = 58.44 g mol⁻¹)
items.correct: Dissolve 2.92 g of NaCl and make up to 100 cm³ of solution.
items.misconception: Add 0.125 mol of NaCl to 250 cm³ of water and stir until dissolved.
items.why:
Everyday mixing (sugar in tea, squash) measures the water added, and informal recipes say 'dissolve in 100 cm³ of water'. Confusing solution with solvent in concentration is widely reported in research on students' ideas about solutions. The volume in C = n/V is the final volume of solution. Use a volumetric flask: dissolve the solute in some water, then add water up to the mark.

Working: Correct procedure: n(NaCl) = 0.500 mol dm⁻³ × 0.100 dm³ = 0.0500 mol; m = nM = 0.0500 mol × 58.44 g mol⁻¹ = 2.92 g, made up to 100 cm³ of solution (equivalently, 0.500 mol dm⁻³ = 29.2 g dm⁻³). 0.500 g ÷ 58.44 g mol⁻¹ = 0.00856 mol, so 0.500 g in 1.00 dm³ gives 0.00856 mol dm⁻³. 0.500 mol in about 0.260 dm³ of solution gives about 1.9 mol dm⁻³. Adding 0.125 mol to 250 cm³ of water gives a solution whose volume is not 250 cm³, so its concentration is not 0.500 mol dm⁻³ (about 0.496 mol dm⁻³: the solution volume is about 252 cm³).
items.specStatementText: The molar concentration is determined by the amount of solute and the volume of solution.
items.random_wrong: Dissolve 0.500 g of NaCl, then make the solution up to 1.00 dm³.
items.working: Correct procedure: n(NaCl) = 0.500 mol dm⁻³ × 0.100 dm³ = 0.0500 mol; m = nM = 0.0500 mol × 58.44 g mol⁻¹ = 2.92 g, made up to 100 cm³ of solution (equivalently, 0.500 mol dm⁻³ = 29.2 g dm⁻³). 0.500 g ÷ 58.44 g mol⁻¹ = 0.00856 mol, so 0.500 g in 1.00 dm³ gives 0.00856 mol dm⁻³. 0.500 mol in about 0.260 dm³ of solution gives about 1.9 mol dm⁻³. Adding 0.125 mol to 250 cm³ of water gives a solution whose volume is not 250 cm³, so its concentration is not 0.500 mol dm⁻³ (about 0.496 mol dm⁻³: the solution volume is about 252 cm³).

items.q: A solution of chlorine in water contains 4.00 g of dissolved chlorine, Cl₂, per dm³. Ignore any reaction of chlorine with water. What is [Cl₂]? (A_r: Cl 35.45)
items.correct: 0.0564 mol dm⁻³
items.misconception: 0.113 mol dm⁻³
items.why:
The periodic table lists one value per element, and the name 'chlorine' is used for both the atom and the molecule, so students do not check which entity the calculation involves. Write the formula of the substance as it exists before calculating M: chlorine gas is Cl₂, oxygen gas is O₂. M is always the molar mass of the entity in the formula used.

Working: M(Cl₂) = 2 × 35.45 = 70.90 g mol⁻¹. [Cl₂] = (4.00 g dm⁻³) ÷ (70.90 g mol⁻¹) = 0.05642 mol dm⁻³ ≈ 0.0564 mol dm⁻³.
items.specStatementText: The molar concentration is determined by the amount of solute and the volume of solution.

items.q: Two identical sealed flasks are at the same temperature and pressure. One is filled with methane, CH₄, and the other with chlorine, Cl₂. The methane flask contains 5.00 × 10²² atoms in total. How many atoms does the chlorine flask contain? (A_r: H 1.01, C 12.01, Cl 35.45)
items.why:
Avogadro's law is often paraphrased using 'particles', which students read as atoms, and they do not distinguish the molecules of a gas from the atoms in them. Avogadro's law counts the independent particles moving in the gas, which are molecules (for noble gases, single atoms). To find atoms, multiply by the atoms in each molecule.

Working: By Avogadro's law the flasks contain equal numbers of molecules. N(CH₄ molecules) = 5.00 × 10²² ÷ 5 = 1.00 × 10²² = N(Cl₂ molecules). Each Cl₂ molecule has 2 atoms, so N(atoms) = 2 × 1.00 × 10²² = 2.00 × 10²². (The A_r values are not needed.)
items.specStatementText: Avogadro’s law states that equal volumes of all gases measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
items.working: By Avogadro's law the flasks contain equal numbers of molecules. N(CH₄ molecules) = 5.00 × 10²² ÷ 5 = 1.00 × 10²² = N(Cl₂ molecules). Each Cl₂ molecule has 2 atoms, so N(atoms) = 2 × 1.00 × 10²² = 2.00 × 10²². (The A_r values are not needed.)

items.q: Sulfur dioxide reacts with oxygen: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g). What volume of oxygen reacts completely with 30.0 cm³ of sulfur dioxide? All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
items.correct: 15.0 cm³
items.misconception: 60.0 cm³
items.why:
The 'reversal error' in turning a relationship into arithmetic is well documented in mathematics-education research, and in stoichiometry students often invert the mole ratio taken from an equation. Write the ratio with labels and check that they cancel, then ask whether the answer should be larger or smaller than the starting value: there are more atoms than molecules, and less O₂ than SO₂ in 2SO₂ + O₂.

Working: At constant T and p, V ∝ n. From the equation, n(O₂) : n(SO₂) = 1 : 2, so V(O₂) = 30.0 cm³ × 1/2 = 15.0 cm³.
items.specStatementText: Avogadro’s law states that equal volumes of all gases measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
items.working: At constant T and p, V ∝ n. From the equation, n(O₂) : n(SO₂) = 1 : 2, so V(O₂) = 30.0 cm³ × 1/2 = 15.0 cm³.

items.q: At the same temperature and pressure, a flask holds 0.640 g of oxygen, O₂, when filled with oxygen and 1.28 g of gas X when filled with X. What is the molar mass of X? (A_r: O 16.00)
items.correct: 64.0 g mol⁻¹
items.misconception: 32.0 g mol⁻¹
items.why:
The periodic table lists one value per element, and the name 'chlorine' is used for both the atom and the molecule, so students do not check which entity the calculation involves. Write the formula of the substance as it exists before calculating M: chlorine gas is Cl₂, oxygen gas is O₂. M is always the molar mass of the entity in the formula used.

Working: Same flask, same T and p, so by Avogadro's law n(X) = n(O₂) = 0.640 g ÷ 32.00 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0200 mol. M(X) = 1.28 g ÷ 0.0200 mol = 64.0 g mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: Avogadro’s law states that equal volumes of all gases measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
items.working: Same flask, same T and p, so by Avogadro's law n(X) = n(O₂) = 0.640 g ÷ 32.00 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0200 mol. M(X) = 1.28 g ÷ 0.0200 mol = 64.0 g mol⁻¹.

items.q: What is the relative formula mass, M_r, of hydrated calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂·4H₂O? (A_r: H 1.01, N 14.01, O 16.00, Ca 40.08)
items.why:
The water is pictured as moisture on the surface of the crystals, and the raised dot separates it visually from the rest of the formula, so it looks like an add-on rather than part of the formula unit. Everything after the dot belongs to the formula unit: add n × M_r(H₂O) = n × 18.02. Heating a hydrate drives this water off, which is why its mass falls.

Working: M_r = 40.08 + 2(14.01 + 3 × 16.00) + 4(2 × 1.01 + 16.00) = 40.08 + 124.02 + 72.08 = 236.18. M_r has no unit.
items.specStatementText: Masses of atoms are compared on a scale relative to ¹²C and are expressed as relative atomic mass A_r and relative formula mass M_r.

items.q: Does one mole of any substance contain 6.02 × 10²³ atoms?
items.correct: Only when the specified entities are atoms. One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ of whichever entity is specified: 1 mol of CH₄ contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules and 5 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²⁴ atoms.
items.misconception: One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms, whatever the substance and whatever its particles are.
items.why: The Avogadro constant is usually introduced with elements such as carbon, and the phrase 'Avogadro's number of atoms' is common, so students attach N_A to atoms rather than to the entity named in the question. Always name the entity: 'one mole of CH₄ molecules'. Then count the atoms (or ions, or electrons) in each entity and multiply.
items.specStatementText: The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly the number of elementary entities given by the Avogadro constant.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does one mole of every substance occupy 22.7 dm³ at 273 K and 100 kPa?
items.correct: No. Only gases (behaving ideally) share a molar volume, 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ at 273 K and 100 kPa. The molar volume of a solid or liquid depends on the substance: 1 mol of liquid water occupies about 18 cm³.
items.misconception: One mole of any substance, in any state, occupies 22.7 dm³ at 273 K and 100 kPa.
items.why: The molar volume of a gas is taught alongside the mole and is memorised as 'one mole occupies 22.7 dm³', losing the condition that the substance is a gas. The equal molar volume of gases follows from Avogadro's law: gas particles are far apart, so the volume depends on the number of particles, not on what they are. In solids and liquids the particles touch, so the volume depends on their size and packing and differs from substance to substance.
items.specStatementText: The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly the number of elementary entities given by the Avogadro constant.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is M_r measured in atomic mass units?
items.correct: No. M_r has no unit. The mass of one molecule can be given in unified atomic mass units (u), for example 44.01 u for CO₂, but M_r is that mass divided by the atomic mass unit (one twelfth of the mass of a ¹²C atom), a pure number.
items.misconception: Relative masses are measured in atomic mass units (amu or u), so M_r(CO₂) = 44.01 amu.
items.why: Many pre-IB courses describe relative masses as values 'in atomic mass units', so the unit is attached to the relative mass rather than to the mass of the particle. Relative means 'compared with a reference': dividing a mass by the reference mass cancels the units. The unit u belongs to the actual mass of a particle, not to A_r or M_r.
items.specStatementText: Masses of atoms are compared on a scale relative to ¹²C and are expressed as relative atomic mass A_r and relative formula mass M_r.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the reference for relative atomic masses natural carbon, with A_r = 12.01?
items.correct: No. The reference is the isotope carbon-12, assigned exactly 12. Natural carbon has A_r = 12.01 because it also contains about 1% carbon-13.
items.misconception: The relative mass scale is based on carbon as found in nature, so the reference mass is 12.01.
items.why: The periodic table shows carbon as 12.01, and students do not separate the element, a mixture of isotopes, from the single isotope chosen as the standard. The standard must be one kind of atom with a fixed mass, so a single isotope is used: ¹²C = 12 exactly. A_r(C) = 12.01 is itself measured on that scale.
items.specStatementText: Masses of atoms are compared on a scale relative to ¹²C and are expressed as relative atomic mass A_r and relative formula mass M_r.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is amount of substance equal to molar mass divided by mass?
items.correct: No: n = m/M. Units check it: g ÷ g mol⁻¹ = mol, whereas M/m would have the unit mol⁻¹.
items.misconception: The relationship between amount, mass and molar mass is used upside down, n = M/m; for example A_r is divided by the percentage by mass when finding an empirical formula.
items.why: Relationships learned as a 'formula triangle' are remembered as a picture rather than from their units, so the places of m and M are easily swapped. Derive the arrangement from the meaning of M, the mass of one mole: the number of moles in a sample is how many times M fits into its mass, n = m/M. Then check the units.
items.specStatementText: Molar mass M has the units g mol⁻¹.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: To convert a concentration in g dm⁻³ into mol dm⁻³, is the value multiplied by the molar mass?
items.correct: No. Divide by M: [X] = (concentration in g dm⁻³) ÷ M. Units: g dm⁻³ ÷ g mol⁻¹ = mol dm⁻³. Multiplying by M converts the other way, from mol dm⁻³ to g dm⁻³.
items.misconception: A concentration in g dm⁻³ is converted into mol dm⁻³ by multiplying it by the molar mass.
items.why: Both conversions 'use the molar mass', and the direction mol → g, which does multiply by M, is usually taught first, so the multiplication is carried over without checking units. Treat each dm³ of solution like a sample: its mass of solute (g) ÷ M gives its amount (mol). Checking that the units come out as mol dm⁻³ catches the error.
items.specStatementText: The molar concentration is determined by the amount of solute and the volume of solution.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the percentages by mass of the elements in a compound give the ratio of their atoms?
items.correct: No. Mass percentages must be divided by the A_r values to give amounts in moles before a ratio of atoms is taken. Conversely, the fraction of atoms that belong to an element is not its percentage by mass: in (NH₄)₂SO₄ nitrogen is 2 of 15 atoms but 21.20% of the mass.
items.misconception: The percentage composition by mass gives the ratio of atoms directly, and the fraction of an element's atoms in a formula is its percentage by mass.
items.why: Percentages are read as 'shares' of the compound, and students do not distinguish a share of the mass from a share of the atoms; when A_r values are similar the two look alike. Atoms of different elements have different masses. Convert mass to amount (÷ A_r) before comparing numbers of atoms, and convert atoms to mass (× A_r) before finding a percentage by mass.
items.specStatementText: The empirical formula of a compound gives the simplest ratio of atoms of each element present in that compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element present in a molecule.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the percentage by mass of an element found by dividing its mass by the mass of the other elements in the compound?
items.correct: No. Percentage by mass = (mass of the element in one formula unit ÷ M_r of the whole compound) × 100. The denominator is the whole compound, including the element itself.
items.misconception: The percentage by mass of an element is its mass divided by the mass of the rest of the compound, × 100.
items.why: Part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios are confused in proportional reasoning, a difficulty widely reported in mathematics-education research. A percentage is a part of a whole. Check that the percentages of all the elements add up to 100%; part-to-part values do not.
items.specStatementText: The empirical formula of a compound gives the simplest ratio of atoms of each element present in that compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element present in a molecule.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a formula such as CH₂O show which atoms are bonded to which?
items.correct: No. Empirical and molecular formulae give only numbers (or the ratio) of atoms. Bonding is shown by structural formulae: in ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, one carbon atom carries three hydrogen atoms and the other carries none.
items.misconception: The formula of a compound shows how its atoms are bonded, so CH₂O means each carbon atom is bonded to two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
items.why: The formulae of the first molecules met, such as CH₄, H₂O and NH₃, happen to match their bonding, so students read every formula as a description of structure. Use the empirical formula for the ratio of atoms, the molecular formula for the numbers of atoms, and a structural formula (such as CH₃COOH) for which atoms are joined.
items.specStatementText: The empirical formula of a compound gives the simplest ratio of atoms of each element present in that compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element present in a molecule.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In n = CV, can V be used in cm³ when C is in mol dm⁻³?
items.correct: No. V must be in dm³ to match mol dm⁻³: 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³.
items.misconception: The volume can be put into n = CV in cm³ directly, whatever the unit of the concentration.
items.why: Pipettes and burettes read in cm³, and students substitute the number they measured without matching it to the unit of the concentration. Write units in every substitution: mol dm⁻³ × cm³ does not give mol. Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.
items.specStatementText: The molar concentration is determined by the amount of solute and the volume of solution.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the amount in moles given by n = V/C?
items.correct: No: n = CV. mol dm⁻³ × dm³ = mol; V/C has the unit dm⁶ mol⁻¹.
items.misconception: The amount of solute is the volume divided by the concentration, n = V/C.
items.why: n = CV is remembered as a 'formula triangle' picture rather than from what concentration means, so the positions of C and V are swapped. Concentration is amount per dm³, so the amount in V dm³ is C × V. A larger volume or a higher concentration must both give more solute.
items.specStatementText: The molar concentration is determined by the amount of solute and the volume of solution.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does [NaCl] denote the amount of NaCl in moles?
items.correct: No. Square brackets denote molar concentration, the amount per unit volume of solution, in mol dm⁻³. [NaCl] = 0.50 mol dm⁻³ tells you nothing about the total amount until the volume is known.
items.misconception: Square brackets around a formula show the amount of that substance in moles, whatever the volume of the solution.
items.why: Brackets are new notation, and students attach them to the quantity they use most often, the amount n. Read [X] as 'concentration of X'. The amount in a given volume is n = [X] × V.
items.specStatementText: The molar concentration is determined by the amount of solute and the volume of solution.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do heavier or larger gas molecules take up more space, so that fewer fit into a given volume?
items.correct: No. In a gas the molecules are far apart and their own volume is a tiny fraction of the gas volume. The volume depends on the number of molecules, the temperature and the pressure, not on the size or mass of the molecules.
items.misconception: Heavier or larger gas molecules take up more space, so a given volume holds fewer of them.
items.why: Students transfer the picture of solids and liquids, where particle size does affect volume, to gases; diagrams also draw gas particles much larger relative to their spacing than they really are. Almost all of a gas is empty space between molecules. That is why equal volumes of different gases, at the same T and p, hold equal numbers of molecules.
items.specStatementText: Avogadro’s law states that equal volumes of all gases measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure have equal masses?
items.correct: No. They contain equal amounts in moles, so their masses are in the ratio of their molar masses: 1 dm³ of CO₂ has about 22 times the mass of 1 dm³ of H₂ (44.01 ÷ 2.02).
items.misconception: Equal volumes of gases under the same conditions have equal masses.
items.why: Students often regard gases as having little or no mass and do not separate the volume of a sample from its mass; 'equal amounts' is also read as 'equal masses'. Equal volumes mean equal numbers of molecules. Mass = amount × molar mass, so the heavier molecules give the heavier sample. This is why a balloon of CO₂ sinks and one of H₂ rises.
items.specStatementText: Avogadro’s law states that equal volumes of all gases measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do gases always react in equal volumes?
items.correct: No. At the same temperature and pressure, the volumes of reacting gases are in the ratio of their coefficients in the balanced equation: in 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃, 2 volumes of SO₂ react with 1 volume of O₂.
items.misconception: Gases react in equal volumes, so 30.0 cm³ of one gas reacts with 30.0 cm³ of another, whatever the equation.
items.why: The 'equal volumes' of Avogadro's law is misremembered as 'equal volumes react', and the coefficients of the equation are not used. Volume of gas ∝ amount in moles at fixed T and p, so use the mole ratio from the equation exactly as for amounts.
items.specStatementText: Avogadro’s law states that equal volumes of all gases measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the number of atoms in a formula unit the sum of the subscripts written in the formula?
items.correct: No. Every element symbol stands for at least one atom, and a symbol with no subscript stands for one. H₂O has 2 + 1 = 3 atoms; NH₃ has 1 + 3 = 4.
items.misconception: The number of atoms in a formula unit is the sum of the written subscripts, so a symbol with no subscript is not counted (H₂O is taken to have 2 atoms).
items.why: The subscript 1 is never written, so only the numbers printed in the formula get added. Difficulties in interpreting the subscripts of chemical formulae are widely reported in chemistry-education research. Count symbol by symbol: each symbol contributes its subscript, and a symbol with no subscript contributes 1. Then multiply by the amount and N_A.
items.specStatementText: The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly the number of elementary entities given by the Avogadro constant.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a hydrate formula such as CuSO₄·5H₂O, can the 5 in front of H₂O be left out of M_r, as a coefficient in an equation is?
items.correct: No. The number after the dot is part of the formula: each formula unit of CuSO₄·5H₂O contains five water molecules, so M_r includes 5 × 18.02 = 90.10.
items.misconception: The number in front of H₂O in a hydrate formula is a coefficient like those in equations, so it is not included in M_r and the water is counted only once.
items.why: When finding M_r of a substance in an equation, students learn to ignore the coefficient in front of its formula (for 2H₂O the M_r used is still 18.02), and they carry that rule over to the number in a hydrate formula. A coefficient in an equation counts separate formula units; the number after the dot in a hydrate counts water molecules inside one formula unit, so it multiplies M_r(H₂O).
items.specStatementText: Masses of atoms are compared on a scale relative to ¹²C and are expressed as relative atomic mass A_r and relative formula mass M_r.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
